papers.title: Elucidating cesium solidification and stabilization mechanisms in nano-gamma-alumina modified cementitious matrices under realistic conditions
papers.abstract: Abstract Ordinary Portland cement (OPC) matrices are widely used in low and intermediate level radioactive waste immobilization; however, improvements in waste loading, workability, durability, and radionuclide retention remain desirable. This work investigates the influence of nano-γ-Al₂O₃ modification on the short-and long-term solidification and stabilization performance of OPC-based cesium-bearing waste forms under ideal and realistic curing conditions. The synthesized nano-γ-Al₂O₃ particles exhibited mesoporous morphology, reactive hydroxylated surfaces, and negative surface charge suitable for cementitious applications. Under ideal curing conditions, nano-γ-Al₂O₃ displayed a non-monotonic dosage-dependent effect on the hydration and solidification behavior due to multi-variable interactions leading to changes in the nano- and matrix-chemical conditions thus affecting the pore-solution chemistry, and hydration pathways. 5 wt.% modified matrix provided improved workability, enhanced volumetric stability, and acceptable mechanical performance. Under realistic curing conditions and maximum waste loading, the 5 wt.% nano-γ-Al₂O₃ matrices maintained their favorable processing. Mineralogical, spectroscopic, and microstructural analyses revealed the formation of Al-rich hydration assemblages, including AFt, AFm, and hydroxo-AFm phases and the presence of more hydroxylated species in the modified matrix. Elemental-ratio distributions in pristine and leached matrices indicated that Cesium binding is primarily associated with C-S-H/C-A-S-H and AFt/AFm hydration products. The results demonstrate that while nano-γ-Al₂O₃ effectively tailors the workability and hydration pathways under representative waste-conditioning conditions, its implementation involves a performance trade-off between processing behavior, mechanical integrity, and long-term cesium retention.

papers.title: Impurity-driven corrosion and redox control of SS316H in molten NaCl–MgCl2 salts
papers.abstract: Molten chloride salts are promising heat transfer and energy-storage media, but corrosion of structural alloys remains challenging. We investigated SS316H in commercial-grade NaCl–MgCl 2 at 700 °C using immersion tests, multiscale characterization, thermodynamic analysis, and multiphysics electrochemical modeling. The 120 and 500 h baseline tests yielded equivalent area-averaged mass-loss corrosion rates of 460 and 470 μm yr −1 , with maximum penetration depths of 67 and 82 μm. Surface and cross-sectional analyses indicate dissolution of both Fe and Cr, while thermodynamic calculations supported a greater tendency for Cr chlorination. Surface Cr enrichment and MgCr 2 O 4 identification were consistent with Cr dissolution followed by secondary formation of MgCr 2 O 4 near the alloy surface, accompanied by MgO accumulation. Fe-containing species were detected in the recovered salt, consistent with Fe dissolution from the alloy. Relative to baseline rates, H 2 /Ar reduced corrosion rates by 36–37% under 234 h sparging and 81% under 500 h cover-gas conditions. An electrochemical model calibrated against measured rates projected impurity-species and corrosion-rate evolution beyond 500 h under stated assumptions. Time-matched tests are needed to quantitatively rank the delivery modes. These results clarify impurity-driven corrosion mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of gas-phase redox control in molten chloride systems.

papers.title: Degradation-front evolution and micromechanical heterogeneity in cement pastes incorporating expansive agents under sodium sulfate attack
papers.abstract: Expansive agents (EAs) are widely used in concrete but have the potential to reshape the physicochemical pathways under external sulfate attack (ESA) due to the internal introduction of calcium-aluminum-sulfur. ESA induces a depth-dependent degradation front that drives progressive microstructural and chemical degradation; however, the evolution of this reaction front in EA-modified systems remains poorly understood. This study analyzed depth-dependent, micro-level alterations, coupling nanomechanical, chemical, and porosity evaluations to elucidate the reaction front in plain and EA-modified cement pastes under ESA. Specimens containing 0% and 8% EA were immersed in 5% sodium sulfate solution for 200 days, and penetration was analyzed at 2 mm, 10 mm, and 20 mm from the surface. Results showed that, despite a ~1 wt% increase in sulfate in the EA-cement, the degradation front remained confined to 13–20 mm. EA incorporation increased the average Ca/Si ratio by 31% (2 mm) and 20% (10 mm) and elevated the Al/Si ratio by 15–45%. Portlandite was depleted in the degradation zone but progressively accumulated toward the interior. In the degradation zones, EA increased homogenized modulus and hardness by 3.4–12.5%, enhanced high-density C-S-H up to fourfold, and more than doubled portlandite/C-S-H, as hydration-released calcium migrated outward and redeposited portlandite. EA addition reduced microporous phase fractions by 19% (2 mm) and 42% (10 mm) and decreased gel porosity by up to 18%, while increasing local alkalinity and calcium activity, which enhanced portlandite buffering and slowed C-S-H decalcification. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the degradation-front evolution of EA-modified cement under ESA.

papers.title: Corrosion resistance inversion of Ni-Mo-Cr and Ni-W-Cr alloys under isothermal oxidation and cyclic NaCl-deposit hot corrosion
papers.abstract: The degradation behaviors of Ni–Mo–Cr GH3535 (7.01 wt.% Cr) and Ni–W–Cr GH3539 (5.70 wt.% Cr) were compared at 700 °C under isothermal oxidation and cyclic NaCl-deposit hot corrosion. The alloys exhibited a performance inversion between the two conditions. During isothermal oxidation, GH3535 showed a lower oxidation rate and a thinner affected region than GH3539. The higher oxidation rate of GH3539 was associated with CrWO 4 formation, which may compete with continued NiCr 2 O 4 formation, along with a W 6+ -related increase in nickel-vacancy concentration that could accelerate outward cation transport. During cyclic hot corrosion, both alloys underwent severe degradation; however, GH3539 showed a lower cumulative material loss under the wash–recoat protocol: the average thickness reductions after 100 h were approximately 42% for GH3535 and 25% for GH3539. Thermodynamic calculations indicate that possible Mo-bearing chlorides and oxychlorides have substantially higher equilibrium vapor pressures than the corresponding W-bearing species. These volatile Mo-bearing intermediates could hinder the retention of a coherent scale on GH3535, while the lower volatility of W-bearing intermediates is consistent with the more adherent scale on GH3539. Nevertheless, GH3539 developed a subsurface Cr- and W-depleted zone. These results demonstrate the environment-dependent roles of Mo and W in low-Cr Ni-based alloys.

papers.title: Role of defect trapping in the enhanced corrosion resistance of Ni–Mo alloys with yttrium and yttrium oxide additions
papers.abstract: Abstract Corrosion of structural alloys remains a critical challenge for advanced molten salt reactors, where aggressive fluoride salts promote continuous dissolution at the salt–metal interface. While most mitigation strategies emphasize thermodynamic stability, kinetic control of atomic transport has received comparatively less attention. Here, we propose a corrosion mitigation strategy based on diffusion control and vacancy trapping by dilute yttrium (Y) solutes and yttrium oxide (Y 2 O 3 ) dispersions in Ni alloys. A combined computational and experimental approach integrates density functional theory (DFT), self-consistent mean-field (SCMF) diffusion modeling, and an impurity trapping model to quantify the impact of defect trapping on effective vacancy mobility. Strong first-nearest-neighbor vacancy–Y binding, off-lattice vacancy configurations, and elevated rotational and dissociation barriers result in pronounced suppression of vacancy diffusivity, while Y 2 O 3 -associated sites treated as fixed traps in the model further reduce the mobile vacancy population. Ni–Mo (NM), Y-modified (NMY), and Y 2 O 3 -containing (NMYO) alloys were tested in molten fluoride salt at 750 ∘ C. Corrosion penetration decreases systematically from NM to NMY to NMYO, consistent with the predicted reduction in vacancy-mediated transport. The same trend is observed in mass change, with net weight loss decreasing from 0.52% for NM to 0.23% for NMY and 0.09% for NMYO. These results are consistent with an alloy-side transport contribution from defect trapping and reduced atomic transport. This study therefore suggests point defect engineering as a promising alloy design strategy for extreme nuclear environments.
